definition: In mathematics, nonlinear programming (NLP), also known as nonlinear optimization, is the process of solving an optimization problem where some of the constraints are not linear equalities or the objective function is not a linear function.
details: An optimization problem is one of calculation of the extrema (maxima, minima or stationary points) of an objective function over a set of unknown real variables and conditional to the satisfaction of a system of equalities and inequalities, collectively termed constraints. It is the sub-field of mathematical optimization that deals with problems that are not linear.

explainer.lead: Nonlinear programming solves optimization problems where the objective or some constraints are not linear. It matters because many real planning and fitting problems do not fit linear assumptions.

tiers.eli5: It is finding the best value of something under rules, when neither the thing you are maximizing nor the rules are straight-line simple.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers formulate the objective and constraints, then use solver packages that handle nonlinearity, often needing good initial guesses. Pitfall: solvers return local optima, and poor starting points or scaling can cause failure to converge.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, find extrema of an objective function of real variables subject to a system of equality and inequality constraints, where the objective or some constraints are nonlinear. Known limits: global optimality is generally not guaranteed, and results depend on formulation and initialization.

explainer.example: Minimizing fuel use over a route with nonlinear speed-dependent costs and constraints on time windows is a nonlinear program.
